messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David is a 57-year-old tutor who came to treatment after years of arranging his life around not being caught off guard. The assault happened when he was in his forties. He described being cornered by another man in a private setting and overpowered, the worst part not only the sexual violation but the moment he realized he could not stop what was happening. What has stayed with him most sharply is the combination of forced physical contact and the absolute loss of control over his own body. Even now he can say certain sensory details with painful precision—the feel of a hand pinning him, the closeness of a male body, the trapped certainty that saying no made no difference—while other parts seem to fall away. He knows there are missing pieces, and when he tries to explain the event aloud, he often stops, frustrated, saying he knows what happened but cannot find words for it. When those sharp fragments break through, they leave him thinking not just that the assault was terrible, but that something in him remains damaged and unreliable if the memory can still seize him so completely.

In the months afterward, David did not simply feel upset; he came to believe the world had changed into a place where safety depended on constant caution. He was certain he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. Once he saw ordinary life through that lens, more and more things began to snag his attention as possible warnings; a man lingering in a doorway, an unexpected touch, even being alone in a room no longer felt neutral enough to ignore. That belief settled alongside another, more painful one: that his own body had become unreliable, something that had failed to protect him and could not be trusted to warn him in time. The memories fed that conclusion. Their clarity made the assault feel undeniable and close, but the blank spaces left him feeling even less secure, as if danger could come from what he did not fully remember as much as from what he did. Over time he also felt increasingly set apart from other people, especially from other men, as though he had been pushed into a private world no one else could quite enter.

Those meanings now shape what catches him in daily life. Because he has come to expect danger and to doubt his own capacity to stay safe, physical touch startles him immediately, being directed or pressured by someone can feel intolerably charged, and being alone with a man is often enough to make his body tense before anything has actually happened. Each time one of these moments catches him, the same conclusion lands with it: that he is still vulnerable, still unable to trust his own body to protect him, and still largely on his own with this. At the tutoring center where he works, he pays close attention to who is in the room and where they are standing. If a male student arrives early and he finds himself alone with him, David begins scanning for signs of threat in the student’s posture, tone, and movements. When parents or staff reach out casually to pat his shoulder in thanks, the contact can pull up the assault with startling force: a vivid flash of the physical restraint, followed by the sickening sense that parts of the memory are still out of reach. In those moments he feels again how little he trusts his body, and the old conviction returns that he is fundamentally alone in managing this.

The memories and the sense of current threat now reinforce each other. The more closely David watches other people for signs they might harm him, the more readily details of the assault spring up. Living in that level of alarm has itself become proof to him that his life is no longer fundamentally safe and that he is not someone who can afford to let his guard down. He chooses seats in waiting rooms, classrooms, and coffee shops with almost ritual precision, always locating the chair that feels most protected and gives him the clearest view of the room. He avoids unfamiliar places because he cannot quickly assess the danger there. That constant surveillance leaves him primed; a man standing too near in a hallway, an unexpected brush of arms, or a situation in which someone else seems to be deciding for him can bring back the assault in sharp fragments. Each resurgence of memory confirms his belief that the threat is still immediate and that vigilance is necessary, while each episode of vigilance seems to sharpen the memory again.

From those beliefs, a pattern of coping has narrowed his life. Because he feels isolated, unable to trust his body, and convinced that strong emotion will overwhelm him, David avoids situations likely to stir much feeling. He keeps conversation with students focused tightly on coursework and declines social invitations from colleagues. He has become notably rigid about physical boundaries, stepping back from handshakes or finding ways to keep a desk between himself and others. Smoking has become another way he manages the internal surge; he describes slipping outside between sessions not for pleasure but to settle himself, to do something familiar when his chest tightens and his thoughts start racing. His monitoring of exits and strangers makes him choose routines over spontaneity, and his avoidance of touch has affected even benign contact, contributing to a life that feels controlled but increasingly small.

What finally brought him in was a recent incident at work when a male student, trying to show him something on a screen, leaned in and touched his forearm. David froze, lost the thread of the lesson, and afterward sat in his car chain-smoking, shaken by how immediately the memory had returned and how complete his fear felt. He was frightened by how powerfully these moments still govern him and by the possibility that he will keep retreating from work and from people until there is very little left. At the same time, he said quietly that he hopes for something simple: to sit in a room without calculating danger, to teach without bracing for touch, and to feel that his body belongs to him again.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not explicitly show triggers causing or intensifying negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
The vignette does not clearly state that David’s negative appraisals lead to intrusive memories within the same paragraph.
The vignette does not clearly convey that David’s negative appraisals make more stimuli become triggers or reminders within the same paragraph.
The vignette does not explicitly show intrusive memories leading to negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
The vignette does not clearly state that David’s sense of threat leads to negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
